title: Deion Sanders' Colorado Stumbles Again: Third Consecutive Loss Shakes Program Momentum
body:
Colorado’s season‑opening surge has evaporated, as head coach Deion Sanders watched his Buffaloes stumble to a third consecutive defeat, a 29‑7 loss to No. 10 Texas Tech on Saturday night. After beginning the 2026 campaign with two convincing victories, the once‑promising Colorado squad found itself trailing at halftime and never recovered, raising questions about the program’s trajectory under the former NFL star’s leadership.

The Red Raiders dominated from the outset, capitalizing on a stout Colorado defense that had looked impenetrable in the first two games. Texas Tech’s offense, orchestrated by senior quarterback Jake Miller, methodically marched down the field, scoring on three of its first four drives. Colorado managed a field goal before the intermission, cutting the deficit to 14‑3, but the momentum shift was unmistakable. In the second half, Texas Tech’s relentless ground attack and a series of timely turnovers forced the Buffaloes into a defensive shell, limiting their offensive opportunities to a handful of short drives that never materialized into points.

Sanders, who entered the college ranks with a high‑profile hiring that promised a cultural overhaul, now faces mounting scrutiny. The Buffaloes entered the season with a revamped recruiting class and a revamped staff, and the early wins against non‑Power Five opponents had fans dreaming of a rapid ascent in the Pac‑12 hierarchy. However, the loss to a top‑ten opponent exposed lingering deficiencies in offensive line protection and secondary coverage—areas that have been the focus of Sanders’ offseason rebuild. “We saw flashes of what we can be,” Sanders said in the post‑game press conference, “but consistency against elite competition is still a work in progress.”

Analysts point to the Buffaloes’ limited depth as a contributing factor. While the starting roster boasts several highly touted freshmen and transfers, the bench lacks seasoned veterans who can sustain performance when the starters tire. Injuries have also taken a toll; senior linebacker Marcus Hayes missed the second half with a hamstring strain, and his absence was felt as Texas Tech’s rushing attack gained yardage in the final quarter. Moreover, Colorado’s offense struggled to establish a rhythm, averaging just 3.5 yards per play and committing three turnovers—a stark contrast to the efficient, high‑tempo style that Sanders has touted as his signature.

The defeat also underscores the competitive landscape of the Big 12 and Pac‑12 crossover schedule. Texas Tech, under head coach Matt Miller, has emerged as a defensive juggernaut, ranking in the top five nationally for points allowed per game. Their ability to stifle Colorado’s play-action passes and force the Buffaloes into three‑and‑out sequences highlighted a gap in Colorado’s game planning. In contrast, the Buffaloes’ earlier wins came against lower‑ranked teams that failed to challenge their defensive schemes, masking vulnerabilities that now require immediate attention.

Looking ahead, Colorado’s next matchup pits them against a mid‑tier conference opponent, offering a chance to rebound and rebuild confidence. Sanders has hinted at adjustments to the offensive playbook, emphasizing a quicker release for quarterback Jalen Carter and incorporating more screen passes to alleviate pressure on the line. Defensive coordinator Chris Miller also noted that the secondary will receive additional coaching on zone coverage to better contain deep threats. If the Buffaloes can translate those tweaks into on‑field execution, they may halt the losing streak and salvage a season that still holds promise despite the early setback. The coming weeks will be a litmus test for Sanders’ ability to adapt, and for Colorado fans, the hope is that the early promise can be reclaimed before the conference grind intensifies.
